questions.q: How does the 3-bit repetition code encode and decode a single bit?
options: It sends the bit once, then sends a checksum of it afterward
It encodes 0 as 000 and 1 as 111, and decodes by majority vote across the 3 received bits
It encodes the bit using a random permutation each time it is sent
It encodes 0 as 001 and 1 as 110, and decodes by XOR of the 3 bits
questions.explain: The repetition code's encoding is simply repeating the bit 3 times (000 or 111); decoding takes whichever value is more common among the 3 received bits.

questions.q: At channel flip probability p=0.10, the lesson's verified table gives a success probability of 0.972000 for the 3-bit code. What does this number represent?
options: The probability that majority vote correctly recovers the original bit, i.e. that fewer than 2 of the 3 bits flipped
The probability that the channel has zero noise
The probability that all 3 bits flip simultaneously
The probability that exactly 1 bit flips
questions.explain: Success means majority vote still returns the correct bit, which happens whenever 0 or 1 of the 3 bits flipped (not 2 or 3) -- computed via the binomial sum in the lesson.

questions.q: Why does the 5-bit repetition code outperform the 3-bit code at the same flip rate p, according to the verified table?
options: There is no real difference; the table values are coincidental
Because 5-bit codes use a completely different decoding rule than 3-bit codes
Because the 5-bit code somehow lowers the channel's actual flip probability p
Because majority vote on 5 bits tolerates up to 2 flips before failing, versus only 1 flip tolerated by the 3-bit code
questions.explain: More repeated copies raise the number of simultaneous flips majority vote can tolerate (floor(n/2)), which is why n=5 beats n=3 at the same p, at the cost of more physical bits used.

questions.q: What is the real cost of using the 5-bit repetition code instead of sending the bit uncoded?
options: It only works for even-length codes
The channel's flip probability p increases as a side effect
5x physical-bit overhead per logical bit protected
No cost at all -- repetition codes are free
questions.explain: The code protects 1 logical bit using 5 physical bits, a 5x overhead -- the same 'more resources for lower error rate' tradeoff this course generalizes to quantum error correction in later chapters.

questions.q: The lesson states that repetition coding can 'backfire' at a high enough flip rate p. What is the underlying reason?
options: Repetition codes always fail once p is nonzero
If p exceeds 0.5, bit flips are more common than non-flips, so the 'majority' outcome is more often wrong than right
The majority-vote formula is undefined for p > 0.1
Repetition codes only work for p exactly equal to 0
questions.explain: The binomial success-probability formula assumes flips are the minority event; once p > 0.5, flips dominate and majority vote systematically picks the wrong value more often than the right one.
